::: {.cite-bar .domain-foreign-policy}
[In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Pub. L. 80-402]{.cite} [62 Stat. 6]{.cite} [22 U.S.C. 1431 et seq.]{.cite}
:::

The legal foundation of U.S. public diplomacy. It authorized the State Department to explain the United States to foreign audiences through broadcasting, publications, and educational and cultural exchanges.

## Key provisions

- Authorized international information activities, including what became the Voice of America.
- Authorized educational and technical exchanges.
- Later amendments barred domestic dissemination of material produced for foreign audiences.
- 2012 amendments allowed that material to be made available in the United States on request, while still barring programs aimed at influencing domestic opinion.

## Why it matters

It draws the line between informing foreign publics and propagandizing Americans, a line that also shapes military information operations. The 2012 change came through [the annual NDAA](ndaa-annual.qmd), and the agency that long ran these programs was folded into State by the [Foreign Affairs Reform Act](farra-1998.qmd).

## Current status

In force as amended by the Smith-Mundt Modernization Act of 2012 (FY2013 National Defense Authorization Act, section 1078).
